script: "Guests begged for beds, hotel denied, and I was forced to charge them.". It was the first night I got a family of four in a King+futon+Jacuzzi room. They checked in, then stormed to the desk, complaining that the room didn't have enough beds for everyone. "We booked a family package," they said, "but this Jacuzzi suite is for couples." I told them we had no double queens left and that a cot would cost extra. They were like, "Why didn't you book a room that actually fits us?" I am like, "The room description never changes just because you're a family." Some other families of five had already booked that same room and added a cot or an inflatable mattress when they booked. They knew the layout. Twenty minutes later, they came back, and I was like, "Okay, what's next?" They said they'd lost their tickets—one family pass for two days, worth over $250. I explained that those tickets are sold in bulk at the start of summer, we pay for them upfront, and if any are left at the end of the season we send them back for a credit. We can't just give them a new one because that's a loss. So I said no. They were stunned. "We booked a package that included entry to this attraction," they shouted. "Your confirmation email says we have a pass. You just gave us a piece of paper. We lost it. We want to go now. What do you do to fix this?" I was at a loss for words. I called my boss. He was also stunned. After a moment of hesitation, he said, "You have to find the ticket." We searched everywhere, checked the email, the confirmation, the paper, and still nothing. He told them, "You want to go now? The attraction closes in an hour, and you're going to waste one day of your two‑day pass." They were furious. "We already wasted time with the bedding situation," they yelled. "Now we lost the ticket because of your archaic paper system. We need a digital version!" The attraction doesn't offer digital tickets, so the boss was stuck. He tried to call the sales director of the attraction. Voicemail. He sent an email. I told the guests we'd have to wait for a reply. They went out for dinner, came back, and hit the desk again. "What do we do now?" they demanded. We had no response from the attraction yet. I said, "We can try to use the last digits of the ticket to cancel and get a credit, or maybe you can go to customer service and get a new one, but we need to wait for their reply. They're closed, so tomorrow." That triggered full‑blown rage mode. "NO I DON'T CARE WHAT THEY SAY! I DID BUSINESS WITH YOU! YOU HAVE TO PROVIDE ME A WAY TO GO THERE TOMORROW MORNING! IT SAYS SO IN MY CONFIRMATION EMAIL!" they screamed. I kept saying, "We gave you the room, we gave you the ticket, that's all we can do. We have to wait for the attraction." They slammed the door, muttering about terrible customer service, about how we didn't think outside the box, about how they'd get a bad review. I kept repeating, "There is nothing more I can do tonight," until they finally left.
